transcript: Meeting header: 2025-05-09 16:00 PT | Duration: ~57 mins | Attendees: Evan Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Helios Head of ML), Jon Park (CTO), Orlando Vega (Platform)
transcript_full:
[00:00] Evan Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're here to lock down the POC acceptance criteria and the benchmark plan for Helios' inference use cases. Um, we'll walk through the success metrics, the go/no-go thresholds, and the reporting format. Priya and I will note the technical bits.

[00:28] Marta Ruiz: Great, thanks Evan. Just to restate our goal — we want to validate that Redwood can run our multi-turn summarization + vector search pipeline within our latency and cost targets, and that quality doesn't regress compared to our current fine-tuned model.

[00:45] Priya Desai: Perfect. Quick clarity on scope: the POC will focus on two workloads. One: mult-turn customer-support summarization (avg prompt length ~350 tokens, expected reply 150-400 tokens). Two: dense embeddings for retrieval at ~512 dimensions, batched at ~64. We'll size bench runs around peak-hour traffic and a representative background load.

[01:15] Jon Park: For us, the hard constraints are p95 latency on generation under 700ms for short replies and under 1.2s for long replies, because the UI needs to feel snappy. Cost target is roughly 40% less per query than our current infra but that's flexible if quality substantially increases.

[01:40] Priya Desai: Noted. We usually separate per-request latency SLAs (p95/p99), throughput targets (concurrent QPS / tokens per second), and quality thresholds (human eval pass rate / automated metrics). For this POC we propose:
- Acceptance metrics: generation p95 <= 850ms (short path), p95 <= 1.4s (long path); embeddings p99 <= 120ms single-request; throughput: sustain 150 concurrent small-gen requests with 90% success within SLO.

[02:16] Marta Ruiz: Those numbers sound in the ballpark. Can we make them more concrete into go / no-go bullets? We want a simple yes/no at the end.

[02:30] Evan Chen: Absolutely. Suggested go/no-go rule: Pass if 3 of 4 pillars meet thresholds: latency, throughput, cost delta, and quality. Each pillar has a primary metric and a secondary check. If only two pass, we enter remediation -> optimize config + rerun. If fewer than two pass, it's a no-go.

[02:50] Orlando Vega: Quick question — when you say cost delta, what's the baseline? We're comparing against our on-prem GPU cluster (NVIDIA A100 pool) including Ops overhead.

[03:05] Priya Desai: Yes, baseline is your reported on-prem cost per 1M tokens over last quarter. We'll need your accounting spreadsheet. For the POC, we'll model cost using Redwood's cost projection spreadsheet — we send a line-item estimate for serving cost and infra overhead. Cost pass condition: per-query unit cost <= 0.6x of baseline (i.e., at least 40% lower), or if higher, quality improvement must justify it as noted.

[03:35] Speaker 4: Sorry, the audio chopped — can you repeat the cost rule?

[03:41] Evan Chen: Sure, cost pass is 40% lower per token compared to your provided baseline OR if not, then quality delta must exceed a human-eval threshold we'll define.

[04:00] Marta Ruiz: About quality — we run human evals for hallucination and relevance. What scoring does Redwood expect?

[04:10] Priya Desai: We recommend a combined quality rubric: Precision/Correctness (0-100), Relevance (0-100), and Hallucination flag (binary). Acceptance: average precision >= 82 and hallucination rate <= 5% across 200 sampled summaries. For embedding recall, run an offline rerank task and require recall@10 >= 0.86 relative to your current model.

[04:46] Jon Park: 200 samples seems small but manageable. Will the POC include humans on our side for labeling?

[04:55] Marta Ruiz: Yes, we'll allocate two annotators for the first pass and then validate with a third if differences exceed threshold.

[05:10] Priya Desai: Good. On instrumentation and reporting: Redwood will provide a benchmark harness in a GitHub repo (we'll link as part of next steps). The harness will emit per-request traces to an S3 bucket and a JSON summary containing p50/p90/p95/p99 for latency, success rate, and per-route token counts. We'll also produce a CSV of raw samples for the 200 human eval items and an aggregated JSON for the quality metrics so your team can ingest into your evaluation dashboards.

[05:45] Orlando Vega: For on-prem or VPC tests, network variability is a big factor. How will you normalize network latency vs infra compute?

[05:58] Priya Desai: We'll run two modes: "local" — where harness runs inside your VPC to measure realistic end-to-end; and "colocated" — Redwood runs the workload from a dedicated cluster in our region to measure baseline serving runtime. We'll also capture network RTT distributions and provide trimmed mean latencies (remove top 1% outliers) to make the compute comparison fair.

[06:25] Marta Ruiz: I want that in the reporting format. Specifically: CSV with columns: timestamp, route, request_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, backend_rtt_ms, error_code. And JSON summary with percentiles for latency and success rate.

[06:44] Evan Chen: Yes that aligns with our templates. We'll include the exact schema in the repo. Priya: can you call out the benchmark scenarios and sample sizes?

[06:56] Priya Desai: Sure. Scenario A: interactive gen (simulate 150 concurrent small sessions) — 10k requests over 30 minutes, 95% within SLO target. Scenario B: bulk embedding ingestion — 50k items batched at 64 over a 2-hour window to measure throughput and per-item latency. Scenario C: mixed background traffic to test autoscaling and cold-cache effects — include KV cache warmup and a cold-start test (restart process and measure first 200 requests separately).

[07:36] Jon Park: For the mixed test, we want to see warm vs cold; our users report variability when cache misses spike. What's Redwood's KV cash strategy?

[07:46] Priya Desai: (laughs) KV cache — yes, sorry — KV cache. We'll instrument cache hits/misses and include cache-priming script in the harness. We'll also try quantized and non-quantized model variants where applicable to show cost vs quality tradeoffs.

[08:04] Marta Ruiz: Good. A couple of redlines from legal/security: we need audit logs and SSE-KMS support for any S3 artifacts. Also SOC2 reports.

[08:17] Evan Chen: We're SOC 2 compatible and support SSE-KMS for artifacts. We'll attach the security pack in the follow-up. For private deployment POC you'll get a limited control plane in your VPC and KMS integration for key sealing.

[08:35] Orlando Vega: On scheduling, what's the target run window? We'd prefer next week but can do the week after.

[08:40] Priya Desai: Technically we can run initial baseline tests as soon as we have the prompt sets and sample logs. Our recommended timeline:
- Day 0-3: exchange artifacts and infra pre-checks (VPC peering, creds)
- Day 4-7: run baseline colocated tests + produce initial report
- Day 8-10: run VPC/on-prem tests and human eval collection
- Day 11: go/no-go review call and sign-off

[09:12] Marta Ruiz: That sounds reasonable. We aim to start pre-checks Monday so the Day 11 review would be mid-next-week.

[09:20] Evan Chen: Let's lock specific acceptance criteria in writing — I'll summarize here and we'll put in a PDF: 
1) Latency: generation p95 <= 850ms (short) and p95 <= 1.4s (long), embeddings p99 <= 120ms.
2) Throughput: sustain 150 concurrent small-gen requests with >= 90% success under SLO; embeddings throughput at least 4k items/min with batch size 64.
3) Cost: unit cost per query <= 0.6x baseline OR demonstrate quality win (see 4).
4) Quality: human eval avg precision >= 82, hallucination rate <= 5% on 200 samples; embedding recall@10 >= 0.86.
Pass rule: at least 3 of the 4 pillars must pass. Secondary checks include operational readiness (audit logs, KMS, SSO) and a clean error rate (<1% 5xx).

[10:05] Jon Park: If we fail one pillar narrowly, do we get a remediation run?

[10:12] Evan Chen: Yes — remediation path: one tuning iteration (quantization changes, batching config, or model variant) and one re-run within the POC window. We agree that the remediation is part of the POC scope. If after remediation we still fail >=2 pillars, then no-go.

[10:28] Marta Ruiz: How will results be reported for sign-off — do we need a specific template?

[10:34] Priya Desai: We'll provide a sign-off packet: 1) Benchmark raw CSVs in S3, 2) JSON summary with percentile tables and heatmaps, 3) a short PDF executive summary with pass/fail per pillar and recommended config, 4) a Jupyter notebook that reproduces the plots and key calculations. We'll ask both technical and business stakeholders to sign off in an email thread or in the CRM record.

[11:00] Speaker 4: Two smaller items — will Redwood run the human eval or do we? And do you support a delta metric for perceived helpfulness?

[11:08] Evan Chen: We can run the human eval if you want — typically customers prefer to run with their annotators to avoid data transfer. We'll provide the annotation schema and an optional quality-review UI. For perceived helpfulness you can add a Likert scale; we can compute delta-helpfulness and include it in the summary.

[11:28] Priya Desai: One more technical note: we'll include tracing IDs in the CSV for correlating a low-level stack trace to the request (e.g., model variant, kernel config). That will help root-cause intermittent outliers.

[11:42] Orlando Vega: Perfect. I'll open the network ticket and share the sample logs. We'll aim to have the prompt sets and two weeks of traffic by Monday.

[11:50] Evan Chen: Great. To recap next steps — Evan to send bench repo + security pack; Helios to upload prompts and logs; Redwood to prepare cost projection; schedule the run and follow-up review. We'll lock the sign-off template and ship the artifacts in one package so sign-off is straightforward.

[12:10] Marta Ruiz: Thanks everyone, this clarifies a lot. Looking forward to the repo and schedule.

[12:18] Evan Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up in-thread with links. Meeting adjourned.
